title: Hippopotamus Attack | The Sensei Speedrun | Grandmaster Naroditsky
openingName: Hippopotamus System (Black vs the double fianchetto)

moves.spoken: White opens with the flank move g3, so we grab the center at once with e5 — a reverse Modern where we get the big pawn share.
teaches: answer a flank opening by taking the center

moves.spoken: White heads for the Hippopotamus, fianchettoing on both wings and conceding the center entirely.

The key move: c6. It's aimed at the fianchettoed light-squared bishop, disarming it by leaving it to bite on granite against a fixed pawn wall — a London-flavored idea, with the bishop coming to d6 next.
teaches: blunt the fianchettoed bishop with a pawn wall

moves.spoken: The bishop to d6 props up the e5-pawn; a later f4 holds no real danger for us here.
White's knight to f3 is already a slight inaccuracy — in the Hippo it belongs on e2, precisely so this doesn't happen.
teaches: the Hippo knight belongs on e2

moves.spoken: And here's why: the pawn to e4 clamps the light squares, seizing space the fianchettoed bishop can no longer contest.
White's knight to e5 is dubious — we're not winning outright, but Black is now solidly the better side.
The harmonious answer is the queen to e7 — natural development that leaves the intruding knight with no squares, so White must lash out with f4 or d4, both weakening.
teaches: improve a piece while trapping his

moves.spoken: An instructive moment: we do NOT capture en passant here. Taking would do the dark-squared bishop and the f3-square a real favor — and our pawn on e4 is exactly what clamps f3 shut. The clamp is worth more than the trade.
teaches: don’t relieve his bad bishop or free f3

moves.spoken: The right way to remove the knight is clinical, not the capture on e5 that would hand over our good bishop — the queen's knight comes to d7 to swap it off instead.
teaches: trade off cleanly, keep your good bishop

moves.spoken: The knight is gone and we've kept everything that matters — the clamp on f3, the intact pawn chain — and now we turn to the kingside attack.
teaches: liquidate the intruder, keep the structure

moves.spoken: No fear of the uncastled king — we can castle long whenever we like, so we start straight in with h5, going for a quick mate on the thematic g3 hook.
teaches: attack with the king in the center when it’s safe
plans: h5-h4 to lever open the g3 hook

moves.spoken: h4 slams into the hook on g3, prying the kingside open.
Opening the h-file is a no-brainer — the rook now points straight at White's king.
With the files open the weaknesses jump out — the e3 and h2 pawns are both falling. The knight to g4 sets up simple, crushing chess.
teaches: open lines expose the weak pawns

moves.spoken: The precise finish isn't grabbing the rook — it's the knight taking on g2 to rip open the h-file, combining winning material with the mating attack. And never take on f1 while our own rook on h8 sits undefended. The light squares decide it: we have a light-squared bishop and White has none.
